CONTEMPT FOR FAILURE TO PAY COURT-ORDERED SUPPORT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Support Contempt Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, whose family law matter is pending, or may be filed, in the California superior court for Fresno County. It describes what California statutes and a published California Supreme Court decision say about the contempt process used to enforce a court order for child, family, or spousal support: which code sections make disobedience of a support order punishable as a contempt of court, how a contempt proceeding is initiated, what the moving party must prove and what the person charged may raise as a defense, how many counts a period of nonpayment can generate, how long the law allows a contempt action to be commenced, what penalties the statutes authorize, and how contempt relates to the separate criminal offense of failing to furnish necessaries for a child. This information sheet states what the law says in general terms. It does not determine whether any support order of Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee was validly made or served, whether any payment was missed, whether any nonpayment was willful, whether either person had the ability to comply, whether any limitations period has run, or what penalty any conduct would draw; those are matters for the court to decide on the specific facts.

THE FAMILY CODE LISTS CONTEMPT AS ONE OF SEVERAL WAYS A FAMILY LAW ORDER MAY BE ENFORCED
Family Code section 290 is the general enforcement provision for orders and judgments made under the Family Code, including support orders. It states that such a judgment or order may be enforced by the court by execution, by the appointment of a receiver, or by contempt, or by any other order the court in its discretion determines from time to time to be necessary. On the face of the section, contempt is one item in a list of enforcement mechanisms rather than the exclusive route, and the section is written permissively (“may be enforced”) and commits the choice of any other necessary order to the court's discretion. The contempt mechanism itself is not defined in the Family Code; it is governed by Title 5 of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the provisions described in this document's later clauses.

DISOBEDIENCE OF A LAWFUL COURT ORDER IS LISTED AS A CONTEMPT OF THE AUTHORITY OF THE COURT
The contempt power is codified in Title 5 of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, sections 1209 through 1222. Section 1209, subdivision (a), opens by stating that the acts or omissions it then lists, taken in respect to a court of justice or proceedings in it, are contempts of the authority of the court. The fifth item on that list is disobedience of any lawful judgment, order, or process of the court. The statutory language is general: it is not limited to family law, and it turns on the judgment or order being a lawful one issued by the court. A court-ordered obligation to pay child, family, or spousal support is an order of the court, and the Family Code separately names contempt as an enforcement mechanism for such orders.

A CONTEMPT NOT COMMITTED IN THE COURT'S PRESENCE IS CHARGED BY AFFIDAVIT, AND A JUDICIAL COUNCIL FORM SATISFIES THAT REQUIREMENT IN FAMILY LAW MATTERS
Code of Civil Procedure section 1211 separates contempts committed in the immediate view and presence of the court, which may be punished summarily on an order reciting the facts, from contempts not so committed. Failing to make a support payment is not conduct occurring in the courtroom, so it falls in the second category. For that category the statute requires that an affidavit be presented to the court or judge setting out the facts constituting the contempt (or, in the alternative, a statement of the facts by referees, arbitrators, or other judicial officers). Subdivision (b) then states that in family law matters, filing the Judicial Council form entitled “Order to Show Cause and Affidavit for Contempt (Family Law)” constitutes compliance with the section.

FOR A CHILD SUPPORT ORDER, PROOF OF THE ORDER, NOTICE, AND NONCOMPLIANCE IS PRIMA FACIE EVIDENCE OF CONTEMPT
Code of Civil Procedure section 1209.5 addresses the showing required in a contempt proceeding based on a child support order. Where a court of competent jurisdiction has made an order compelling a parent to furnish support, or necessary food, clothing, shelter, medical attendance, or other remedial care for the parent's child, the section states that three things together are prima facie evidence of a contempt of court: proof that the order was made, filed, and served on the parent (or, alternatively, proof that the parent was present in court when the order was pronounced); and proof that the parent did not comply with the order. The section's terms do not include the parent's financial ability to comply among the matters the moving party must prove.

THE CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT HELD THE ELEMENTS ARE A VALID ORDER, KNOWLEDGE, AND NONCOMPLIANCE, AND THAT INABILITY TO COMPLY IS AN AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE
In Moss v. Superior Court (1998) 17 Cal.4th 396, the California Supreme Court reviewed a child support contempt proceeding and addressed how the burden of proof is allocated. The court stated that the elements of this contempt are only a valid court order, the alleged contemner's knowledge of the order, and noncompliance, and that if the petitioner proves those elements beyond a reasonable doubt the violation is established. The court further stated that ability to comply with a support order is not an element that the petitioner must prove beyond a reasonable doubt, and that inability to comply is instead an affirmative defense which the alleged contemner must prove by a preponderance of the evidence. The court described the Legislature as having made that allocation through Code of Civil Procedure section 1209.5, and it disapproved a Court of Appeal decision, In re Feiock (1989) 215 Cal.App.3d 141, to the extent that decision had treated ability to pay as an element the petitioner must prove.

THE CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT HELD THAT CONTEMPT MAY REST ON A PARENT'S WILLFUL FAILURE TO SEEK AND ACCEPT AVAILABLE EMPLOYMENT
The central holding of Moss v. Superior Court (1998) 17 Cal.4th 396 concerned a parent who was unemployed and therefore, as a matter of present cash, unable to pay the ordered child support. Older authority had been read to mean that punishing such a parent would amount to involuntary servitude or to imprisonment for debt. The California Supreme Court concluded that there is no constitutional impediment to imposing contempt sanctions on a parent for violating a judicial child support order when the parent's financial inability to comply is the result of the parent's willful failure to seek and accept available employment commensurate with his or her skills and ability. Two features of that holding appear in its own words: the failure to seek and accept work must be willful, and the employment in question must be available and commensurate with the parent's skills and ability. The court nonetheless affirmed the judgment in the case before it, reasoning that because its holding might be deemed an unanticipated change in the law given the earlier understanding, the custodial parent had not carried her burden under the law as it had been understood.

THE GENERAL CONTEMPT PENALTY PROVISION: A FINE, UP TO FIVE DAYS IN JAIL, AND ATTORNEY'S FEES AND COSTS TO THE PARTY WHO BROUGHT THE PROCEEDING
Code of Civil Procedure section 1218, subdivision (a), states the general disposition of a contempt proceeding. On the answer and the evidence taken, the court or judge determines whether the person proceeded against is guilty of the contempt charged. If the person is adjudged guilty, the statute authorizes a fine of not more than one thousand dollars ($1,000) payable to the court, or imprisonment of not more than five days, or both. The same subdivision adds a fee-shifting provision: a person who is subject to a court order as a party to the action, or that person's agent, who is adjudged guilty of contempt for violating that order may be ordered to pay the party who initiated the contempt proceeding the reasonable attorney's fees and costs that party incurred in connection with the proceeding.

In addition, a person who is subject to a court order as a party to the action, or any agent of this person, who is adjudged guilty of contempt for violating that court order may be ordered to pay to the party initiating the contempt proceeding the reasonable attorney’s fees and costs incurred by this party in connection with the contempt proceeding."

FOR CONTEMPT OF A FAMILY CODE ORDER, THE STATUTE PRESCRIBES AN ESCALATING COMMUNITY SERVICE AND IMPRISONMENT SCHEME, WITH PROBATION AS AN ALTERNATIVE
Code of Civil Procedure section 1218, subdivision (c), applies where a party is found in contempt of court for failure to comply with a court order made under the Family Code. Subject to the sentencing option in paragraph (2), the statute directs the court to order an escalating disposition measured per count of contempt: on a first finding, community service of up to 120 hours or imprisonment of up to 120 hours; on a second finding, community service of up to 120 hours in addition to imprisonment of up to 120 hours; and on a third or any subsequent finding, imprisonment of up to 240 hours and community service of up to 240 hours, together with an administrative fee not exceeding the actual cost of administering and supervising the contemner in a community service program. The statute also directs the court to take the parties' employment schedules into consideration when ordering community service or imprisonment or both. Paragraph (2) supplies an alternative: in lieu of imprisonment, community service, or both, the court may grant probation or a conditional sentence, for a period not exceeding one year on a first finding, two years on a second, and three years on a third or any subsequent finding; the statute gives “probation” and “conditional sentence” the meanings set out in Penal Code section 1203, subdivision (a).

EACH UNPAID MONTH MAY BE CHARGED AS A SEPARATE COUNT, AND THE STATUTE SETS A THREE-YEAR WINDOW FOR SUPPORT CONTEMPTS
Code of Civil Procedure section 1218.5 contains two rules specific to contempts alleging nonpayment of support. First, where the contempt alleged is failure to pay child, family, or spousal support, each month for which payment has not been made in full may be alleged as a separate count of contempt, and punishment may be imposed for each count proven — which is what connects this section to the per-count penalties in section 1218. Second, the section sets the period of limitations for commencing a contempt action: three years from the date that the payment was due where the contempt alleged is failure to pay child, family, or spousal support, and two years from the time the alleged contempt occurred where the action before the court is enforcement of another order under the Family Code.

A PARTY IN CONTEMPT IS BARRED FROM ENFORCING A DISSOLUTION ORDER, BUT THAT BAR DOES NOT APPLY TO CHILD OR SPOUSAL SUPPORT ORDERS
Code of Civil Procedure section 1218, subdivision (b), states a consequence of being in contempt that operates apart from any penalty. A party who is in contempt of a court order or judgment in a dissolution of marriage, dissolution of domestic partnership, or legal separation action is not permitted to enforce such an order or judgment against the other party, by way of execution or otherwise, either in the same action or by way of a separate action. The subdivision then carves out support: the statute states that this restriction does not affect and does not apply to the enforcement of child or spousal support orders. On the face of the statute, then, a party's own contempt does not disable that party from enforcing a child or spousal support order.

This restriction shall not affect nor apply to the enforcement of child or spousal support orders."

THE UNDERLYING SUPPORT JUDGMENT ITSELF IS ENFORCEABLE UNTIL PAID IN FULL AND IS EXEMPT FROM RENEWAL
The contempt limitations periods are not the same thing as the life of the support judgment. Family Code section 4502 states that the period for enforcement and the procedure for renewal of a judgment or order for child, family, or spousal support are governed by Family Code section 291. Section 291, in turn, states that a money judgment made or entered under the Family Code, including a judgment for child, family, or spousal support, is enforceable until paid in full or otherwise satisfied; that such a judgment is exempt from any requirement that a judgment be renewed; and that failure to renew has no effect on the judgment's enforceability.
